newsitem.title: USA: Kemp and Gore clash on ethics issue.
newsitem.headline: Kemp and Gore clash on ethics issue.

text.p: Republican vice presidential candidate Jack Kemp on Sunday accused the Clinton White House of abuse of power and Vice President Al Gore accused Kemp of taking the low road in the election campaign.
The question of ethics wove through TV appearances by political figures as President Bill Clinton campaigned in Denver and Republican candidate Bob Dole was on the stump in New Jersey.

The issues were raised three days before Clinton and Dole are to have their second and final televised debate. Both Dole and Kemp avoided attacks on Clinton ethics in their earlier separate debates with Clinton and Gore.
Clinton flew to Albuquerque, New Mexico, on Sunday to prepare for his debate in San Diego, California, on Wednesday.

Appearing on ABC's "This Week With David Brinkley" program, Kemp said, "It is clear that Travelgate and Filegate, the abuse of power, the arrogance of power, the possibility of a pardon (for Clinton's Whitewater partners) are not the type of things that we would want or expect from the Oval Office of the president of the United States."

Travelgate is shorthand for the firing of the staff of the White House travel office and Filegate referred to the improper acquisition of hundreds of FBI files on Republicans by the personnel security office in Clinton's White House.
Gore said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that Kemp had yielded to the urgings of the Dole campaign to "take this kind of low road attack."
"They pledged they would not do that. And they just flip-flopped on that," he said in response to similar remarks made by Kemp Saturday in a radio address.
Deputy White House chief of staff Harold Ickes called the ethics attack "a sign of desperation on the part of the Dole campaign" that would not benefit the Republican contender.

Meanwhile, House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich predicted that congressional and criminal investigations would be launched into an Indonesian businessman's $425,000 contribution to the Democratic Party.
Gingrich also linked reports of alleged drug use by some members of the White House staff to what he said were administration cutbacks in the anti-drug war.

Gingrich's comments on CBS's "Face the Nation" program drew a sharp retort from Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart who said in Denver: "I think Speaker Gingrich ought to look deep inside before he talks about ethical issues."
Gore also challenged Dole to submit his proposed budget plan featuring a 15 percent tax cut to the Congressional Budget Office for its analysis before the election.
Dole campaign spokesman Nelson Warfield said the Dole budget would be sent to the CBO "when the time comes to submit a budget" next January.
But Kemp, questioned about having the Dole budget plan submitted to the CBO now, said he had no problem about such a course, adding: "We'll do it."

Gingrich, in his TV interview, quoted an account by a former White House-assigned FBI agent on alleged drug use, adding: "It helps you understand why, as soon as they got sworn into office, they cut the office of the drug czar by 82 percent and why they cut drug interdiction by 50 percent."

Gingrich also predicted "unavoidable" investigations by Congress and by an independent counsel of a $425,000 campaign contribution to the Democratic Party by an Indonesian couple, that has been acknowledged by the Democratic National Committee.
Gore said the contribution was lawful.
